requirements: The core contributions of 'The Polar Express: Optimal Matrix Sign Methods and Their Application to the Muon Algorithm' have been reproduced. This comprises: (1) the Polar Express algorithm itself, i.e. the greedy per-iteration minimax construction of Theorem 3.1, the degree-3 closed form and degree-5 Remez solvers that realize it, and the finite-precision stabilizations that make it usable in bfloat16; (2) its convergence advantage over degree-5 Newton-Schulz and the heuristic methods of Jordan et al. (2024b) and Cesista et al. (2025) on synthetic and GPT-2 gradient matrices; (3) its integration into the Muon optimizer, yielding consistently lower validation loss when training GPT-2-Small and GPT-2-Large on FineWeb data across all learning rates; and (4) the supporting ablations and appendix experiments, including the insensitivity of Muon to small singular directions, the image classification results, and the auxiliary algorithmic ideas of Appendices I and J.

sub_tasks.requirements: The offline stage of Polar Express has been implemented: the greedy interval recurrence of Theorem 3.1, the per-iteration minimax solvers for degree 3 (closed form, equation (17)) and degree 5 (Remez exchange, Algorithm 2 / Implementation 2), the driver that chains them into a coefficient schedule, and the finite-precision stabilizations of Section 3.4 and Appendix G.

The greedy interval recurrence of Theorem 3.1 has been implemented: starting from [l_1, u_1] = [l, u], each iteration t selects the minimax-optimal odd polynomial p_t on the current interval, then advances the interval via l_{t+1} = p_t(l_t) and u_{t+1} = 2 - l_{t+1}. The composition p* = p_T o ... o p_1 is the globally optimal approximation to the constant function 1 on [l, u] among all compositions of T odd polynomials of degree d.

At each iteration t, the code selects p_t by solving the minimax subproblem arg min_{p in P_d^odd} max_{x in [l_t, u_t]} |1 - p(x)| on the CURRENT interval [l_t, u_t], i.e. the best uniform approximation to the constant function f(x) = 1 from odd polynomials of degree at most d, as specified in Theorem 3.1 equation (8).

The polynomial applied at iteration t differs from the polynomial applied at iteration t' != t (for early iterations, before the interval has collapsed). That is, the implementation adapts the update rule per iteration rather than reusing a single fixed polynomial for all T iterations as Newton-Schulz does, which is the defining structural difference stated in Section 1.3 and Appendix B.
The offline recurrence is initialized with l_1 = l, where l is the user-supplied lower bound on the singular values of the input matrix, as specified in Theorem 3.1.

The offline recurrence is initialized with u_1 = u, where u is the user-supplied upper bound on the singular values of the input matrix (u = 1 for the paper's default configuration), as specified in Theorem 3.1.

After p_t is found, the new lower bound is computed as the scalar evaluation l_{t+1} = p_t(l_t), per equation (10). This is a single scalar polynomial evaluation and must NOT be implemented as a search for min_{x in [l_t, u_t]} p_t(x) over a grid or as any matrix computation.

After l_{t+1} is computed, the new upper bound is obtained from the symmetry relation u_{t+1} = 2 - l_{t+1}, per equation (10), rather than by evaluating p_t(u_t) or maximizing p_t over the interval. This relation follows from the equioscillation property that the image of [l_t, u_t] under p_t is centered on 1.
The per-iteration worst-case error max_{x in [l_t, u_t]} |1 - p_t(x)| is obtained as 1 - l_{t+1}, per equation (10), and is available (returned or logged) at each offline step.
After the offline loop completes, the final worst-case error 1 - l_{T+1} of the composition p* is computed and exposed (returned or logged), per equation (9).

The T stored polynomials are applied in the order p_1, p_2, ..., p_T (the polynomial derived from the widest interval is applied first), so that the realized composition is p* = p_T o p_{T-1} o ... o p_1 as defined in equation (3).

The implementation reflects Remark 3.2: the per-iteration degree need not be constant across iterations (a sequence d_1, ..., d_T is admissible), and the paper's choice of a fixed d_t = 5 for all t is a deliberate default justified by Lee et al. (2022, Table 2) rather than a requirement of Theorem 3.1. This is either supported in code (degree is a per-iteration parameter) or documented.

The claimed optimality of equation (9) is numerically verified: the value 1 - l_{T+1} produced by the scalar offline recurrence agrees (to numerical tolerance) with the directly measured max_{x in [l, u]} |1 - p*(x)| obtained by densely sampling the composed polynomial p* on [l, u].

Starting from the same initial interval [l, u] and using the same degree d and iteration count T, the greedy composition attains a strictly smaller worst-case error than T applications of the fixed degree-d Newton-Schulz polynomial, confirming the Section 3.1 claim that Polar Express is strictly faster than Newton-Schulz.

When the lower bound is tight (sigma_min(M) = l), Polar Express reaches any given error level in approximately half the iterations required by Newton-Schulz of the same degree, matching the Section 3.1 claim that the method is 'about twice as fast as Newton-Schulz' in this regime (cf. Chen & Chow (2014, Section 3.1)).

Figure 2 has been reproduced: the first three optimal polynomials p_1, p_2, p_3 for degree d = 5 with l_1 = 0.03 and u_1 = 1 are plotted, each over its own interval, together with the horizontal reference line y = 1 and the induced bounds l_{t+1} = p_t(l_t) and u_{t+1} = 2 - l_{t+1} marked on the axes.
Figure 2 shows that the interval [l_t, u_t] contracts toward 1 as t increases, with each successive polynomial p_t equioscillating about y = 1 over a strictly narrower interval than its predecessor.

The convergence rate guarantee of Theorem 3.3 has been empirically verified: for a matrix normalized so that sigma(M) is contained in [l, 1] and d = 2q + 1, the composed method satisfies ||polar(M) - X_T||_2 <= |1 - l^2|^{(q+1)^T}, giving quadratic convergence for d = 3 and cubic convergence for d = 5.

For a test matrix M normalized so that sigma(M) is contained in [l, 1], the measured spectral norm error ||polar(M) - X_T||_2 is verified to satisfy the Theorem 3.3 bound |1 - l^2|^{(q+1)^T} for a range of T, where d = 2q + 1 is the per-iteration polynomial degree.
For d = 5 (q = 2), the measured error decreases with order of convergence 3 (cubic): the exponent on the error bound triples with each additional iteration, matching Theorem 3.3.
For d = 3 (q = 1), the measured error decreases with order of convergence 2 (quadratic), matching Theorem 3.3.

The spectral norm error bound of equation (11), ||polar(M) - X_T||_2 <= 1 - l_{T+1}, is verified numerically against the true spectral norm error for a test matrix M whose singular values lie in [l, u], using the l_{T+1} produced by the offline recurrence.

The closed-form solution to the per-iteration minimax problem (13) for degree d = 3, given by equation (17), has been implemented: p(x) = beta * p_NS(alpha * x) where p_NS(x) = (3/2)x - (1/2)x^3, alpha = sqrt(3 / (u^2 + l*u + l^2)) and beta = 4 / (2 + l*u*(l + u)*alpha^3).
The scaling factor is computed as alpha = sqrt(3 / (u^2 + l*u + l^2)) from the current interval endpoints, exactly as in equation (17).
The amplitude factor is computed as beta = 4 / (2 + l*u*(l + u)*alpha^3), exactly as in equation (17).
The returned cubic is assembled as p(x) = beta * p_NS(alpha * x) with p_NS(x) = (3/2)x - (1/2)x^3, i.e. as a rescaled Newton-Schulz cubic rather than as an independently parameterized cubic.

The degree-3 coefficients are obtained analytically in closed form, with no Remez exchange loop, root-finding loop, or numerical optimizer invoked, consistent with Section 3.2's statement that an explicit closed-form solution exists for d = 3.

The returned cubic is verified to satisfy the three-point equioscillation conditions of equation (16): p(l) = 1 - E, p(sqrt(-a / (3b))) = 1 + E, and p(u) = 1 - E for a common E, where the interior point sqrt(-a/(3b)) equals 1/alpha and E = beta - 1.
For u = 1, the polynomial x -> p_NS(alpha * x) produced by equation (17) is verified to coincide with the polynomial derived by Chen & Chow (2014), as stated at the end of Appendix F.

Algorithm 2 / Implementation 2, the degree-5 minimax solver for problem (13), has been implemented as a Remez exchange specialized to odd quintics approximating the constant function 1 on [l, u]. It returns coefficients (a, b, c) of p*(x) = a*x + b*x^3 + c*x^5 that minimize max_{x in [l, u]} |1 - p(x)|.

The solver encodes that the optimal odd quintic must equioscillate at exactly 4 points in [l, u], following Lemma C.1 with q = 2 (q + 2 = 4 points), and correspondingly solves for 4 unknowns (a, b, c, E). The number of equioscillation points is fixed by this structural argument, not treated as a tunable parameter.

The two interval endpoints are held fixed as equioscillation nodes across every exchange iteration (x_0^(k) = l and x_3^(k) = u for all k). Appendix F justifies this: an odd quintic has at most two local extrema on the positive real line, so the remaining two equioscillation points must be the endpoints. The exchange loop must never move these two nodes.

The two interior trial points are initialized to x_1^(1) = (3/4)l + (1/4)u and x_2^(1) = (1/4)l + (3/4)u, as prescribed in Appendix F and used in Implementation 2, before the first exchange iteration.

At each exchange iteration k the solver builds and solves the 4x4 linear system of equation (19) whose rows are [x_i, x_i^3, x_i^5, s_i] evaluated at the four current nodes {l, x_1^(k), x_2^(k), u}, with right-hand side [1, 1, 1, 1], recovering (a_k, b_k, c_k, E_k) in one linear solve.

The sign column of the linear system alternates as (+1, -1, +1, -1) across the four nodes, encoding the equioscillation conditions of equation (18): p_k(l) = 1 - E_k, p_k(x_1^(k)) = 1 + E_k, p_k(x_2^(k)) = 1 - E_k, p_k(u) = 1 + E_k.

The interior nodes are refreshed by locating the stationary points of the error e_k(x) = 1 - p_k(x), i.e. by solving 5*c_k*y^2 + 3*b_k*y + a_k = 0 in y = x^2 via the quadratic formula and taking positive square roots, giving x_{1,2}^(k+1) = sqrt((-3*b_k -/+ sqrt(9*b_k^2 - 20*a_k*c_k)) / (10*c_k)), as described in Appendix F and implemented in Implementation 2.

The exchange loop terminates when the error level stabilizes, i.e. when | |E_k| - |E_{k-1}| | falls below a tolerance on the order of double-precision machine epsilon (1e-15 in Implementation 2), rather than after a hard-coded fixed number of passes.

When the interval is nearly degenerate the solver short-circuits: if l/u >= 1 - eps_double^(1/3) (implemented as the test 1 - 5e-6 <= l/u in Implementation 2), the Vandermonde system of equation (19) is ill-conditioned and is bypassed entirely.

In the degenerate branch the solver returns the scaled Newton-Schulz / Pade coefficients ((15/8)/u, (-10/8)/u^3, (3/8)/u^5), i.e. the polynomial (x/u)/8 * (15 - 10(x/u)^2 + 3(x/u)^4), which Appendix F shows is within double-precision machine epsilon of the true optimum in this regime.
The solver returns the three coefficients (a, b, c) of p*(x) = a*x + b*x^3 + c*x^5 as its output, in a form directly consumable by the offline driver that assembles coeffs_list.

All offline coefficient computation (linear solves, root extraction, error levels) is carried out in double precision (float64 / numpy default), consistent with Section 3.5's statement that the polynomials are precomputed in full precision even though the online stage runs in bfloat16.

The exchange loop is observed to converge within five iterations on the intervals arising in the paper's configuration, matching the statement in Appendix F that the authors never observed Algorithm 2 taking more than five iterations to converge.

For a representative interval [l, u], the returned quintic is verified numerically to equioscillate: |1 - p*(x)| attains the same extreme value E with alternating sign at the four nodes, and max_{x in [l,u]} |1 - p*(x)| = |E|.

The offline driver (the optimal_composition routine of Implementation 2 / the offline block of Algorithm 1) has been implemented: it walks t = 1, ..., T, calls the per-iteration solver on the current interval, applies the finite-precision corrections, advances the interval, and accumulates the coefficient list that the online stage consumes.
The driver runs exactly T iterations, invoking the per-iteration optimal polynomial solver once per iteration with the current interval, and accumulating one coefficient tuple per iteration.
When d = 3 the driver dispatches to the closed-form degree-3 routine of equation (17) with the current interval [l_t, u_t] as input.
When d = 5 the driver dispatches to the degree-5 Remez solver (Algorithm 2 / Implementation 2) with the current interval [l_t, u_t] as input.

The lower endpoint passed to the solver is cushioned as max(l_t, cushion * u_t) rather than l_t itself, so that the solver never sees an interval with an extremely small ratio l_t/u_t. This is line 4 of Algorithm 1 and the max(l, cushion*u) call in Implementation 2.

The cushion constant used matches the paper's implementation: Algorithm 1 states the threshold as u_t/10, while Implementation 2 uses the specific value 0.02407327424182761, with Appendix G noting explicitly that 'the choice of 10 is somewhat arbitrary' and that a different factor is used in Implementation 2.

Because cushioning solves the minimax problem on [cushion*u, u] rather than on [l, u], the resulting polynomial is recentered about 1 with respect to the true endpoints by rescaling all three coefficients by 2 / (p(l) + p(u)), so that 1 - c*p(l) = c*p(u) - 1. This is the rescalar step in Implementation 2.

After each iteration the driver advances the interval using the coefficients it just produced: l <- a*l + b*l^3 + c*l^5 and u <- 2 - l, so that the next call to the solver receives the contracted interval. This chaining is what makes the schedule adaptive.
The driver returns an ordered list of T coefficient tuples (one per iteration), structured for direct reuse by the online stage (the coeffs_list of Implementation 1).

The offline stage is run once and its output persisted (hard-coded, cached, or serialized); subsequent calls to the online polar factor routine reuse the stored coefficients and do not re-solve any minimax problem, consistent with Section 3.5.

Running the offline stage with l = 1e-3, u = 1 reproduces the coefficient triples published in Implementation 1 to at least 4 significant figures, beginning with (8.28721201814563, -23.595886519098837, 17.300387312530933) for the first iteration and (4.107059111542203, -2.9478499167379106, 0.5448431082926601) for the second.

The generated coefficient sequence converges to the degree-5 Newton-Schulz coefficients (1.875, -1.25, 0.375) = (15/8, -10/8, 3/8) at later iterations, as reflected by the final entry of coeffs_list in Implementation 1 and by the comment that subsequent coefficients are numerically equal to this triple.

The first polynomial in the generated schedule has a far larger linear coefficient than the Newton-Schulz value 15/8 (approximately 8.29 for l = 1e-3), reflecting the design goal stated in Section 1.3 of prioritizing rapid growth of the smallest singular values in the early iterations.

The finite-precision stabilizations of Section 3.4 and Appendix G are applied during the offline stage: a 1.01 safety factor guards against round-off pushing singular values above u_t, and cushioning of the lower endpoint enforces a lower bound on p_t(x)/x to prevent non-monotonic mapping of singular values.

Each polynomial p_t is replaced by x -> p_t(x / 1.01), implemented by dividing the coefficients as (a / 1.01, b / 1.01^3, c / 1.01^5), consistent with Section 3.4, line 5 of Algorithm 1, and the coefficient rescaling in Implementation 1.

The safety factor is omitted for the final polynomial in the schedule, so the last coefficient tuple is left unscaled. Appendix G explains this correction is needed because the safety factor otherwise causes singular values to converge to approximately 0.999998 rather than to 1.

The implementation guards specifically against the failure mode described in Appendix G, in which a singular value slightly exceeding u_t satisfies p_t(u_t + eps) > u_{t+1} + eps and therefore diverges to infinity over many iterations rather than converging to 1.

With cushioning applied at the u_t/10 threshold, the resulting update polynomials are verified to satisfy p_t(x)/x >= 0.236 on the domain of interest, the bound stated in Appendix G that prevents the loss-of-precision failure identified by Nakatsukasa & Higham (2012).

The stabilized polynomials never map a singular value to a negative value on the working domain, avoiding the extreme failure case described in Appendix G where p_t(sigma_i) < 0 flips the sign of the i-th singular vector and causes convergence to the polar factor of the wrong matrix.

Figure 7 has been reproduced: the unstabilized optimal degree-5 polynomial for the interval [0.005, 1] and its stabilized counterpart are plotted on the same axes over x in [0, 1], together with the reference line 0.236x and horizontal markers at l_{t+1} and u_{t+1}.
Figure 7 shows that the unstabilized optimal polynomial for [0.005, 1] maps singular values near 0.8 down to almost zero, the non-monotonicity that motivates cushioning.

Figure 7 shows that the unstabilized polynomial maps 1 + eps to approximately u_{t+1} + 25*eps, amplifying round-off overshoot by roughly 25x, whereas the stabilized version maps all x <= 1.01 to at most u_{t+1}.

The online stage of Polar Express has been implemented, together with the singular value bound prescription of Section 3.3 that instantiates it: normalization, bfloat16 execution, Horner evaluation of the precomputed odd polynomials using only matrix-matrix products, and the practical engineering details of Implementation 1.

The upper and lower bounds on the singular values required to instantiate the method are chosen as prescribed in Section 3.3: the matrix is rescaled by its Frobenius norm so that u = 1, and the lower bound is guessed as l = 1e-3, motivated by the bfloat16 machine epsilon.

The upper bound on the singular values is obtained by rescaling M by ||M||_F and setting u = 1. Section 3.3 justifies this as a valid (if loose) upper bound that is tight up to a small constant in practice because gradient matrices of dense layers have small effective rank (Yang et al., 2024).
The lower bound is set to l = 1e-3 for the bfloat16 configuration used in all GPT-2 experiments, as specified in Section 3.3 and in the recommendation of Section 3.5.

The choice of l is tied to the working precision as described in Section 3.3: bfloat16 has eps_mach = 2^-8 which is approximately 3.91e-3, and singular values of matrices stored in floating point are usually larger than machine precision (Boutsikas et al., 2024), so l = 1e-3 is chosen just below eps_mach. This rationale is reflected in code or documentation rather than l being an unexplained magic constant.

Because the same [l, u] is used for every input matrix, the polynomial schedule is precomputed once and applied to arbitrarily many inputs, as stated at the end of Section 3.3. The online routine does not recompute bounds or polynomials per call.
The method is verified to converge for any l in (0, u], and an error of one order of magnitude in l delays convergence by only a few iterations, matching the robustness claim in Section 3.3.

The online stage of Polar Express (Algorithm 1 lines 10-14 / Implementation 1) has been implemented: the input is normalized, cast to bfloat16, and the precomputed polynomials are applied in sequence using only matrix-matrix products evaluated by Horner's rule.

The iteration is initialized as X_0 = M / (||M||_F + 1e-2), i.e. the Frobenius norm is offset by 1e-2 rather than used directly. Appendix G states this third finite-precision fix is copied from the original Muon implementation, and it appears as line 10 of Algorithm 1.

Implementation 1's concrete normalization X <- X / (||X||_F * 1.01 + 1e-7) is reproduced, which folds the 1.01 safety factor into the normalization and uses a 1e-7 floor to avoid division by zero on an all-zero gradient.

Odd powers of a rectangular matrix are formed via the identity M^{2q+1} = M(M^T M)^q from Section 2, so that p(M) = a_0*M + a_1*M(M^T M) + ... + a_q*M(M^T M)^q. The implementation never forms an explicit SVD to evaluate the polynomial.

Only odd polynomials are used. Footnote 2 of Section 2 explains that even powers of the singular values of a non-symmetric or rectangular matrix cannot be formed without an explicit SVD, so the admissible search space is restricted to P_d^odd throughout.

Each iteration is evaluated by Horner's rule rather than by forming X^3 and X^5 separately and summing. Either of the two equivalent factorizations is acceptable: the form written in Section 3.5, X_t = X_{t-1} * (a*I + Y*(b*I + c*Y)) with Y = X_{t-1}^T X_{t-1}, or the mirrored form used in Implementation 1, X_t = a*X_{t-1} + (b*A + c*A@A) @ X_{t-1} with A = X_{t-1} X_{t-1}^T, which is the cheaper of the two once the transpose optimization has made the iterate wide. Either way exactly three matrix-matrix products are performed per degree-5 iteration.

The online stage uses only matrix-matrix products and linear combinations of matrices. No matrix inverse, QR decomposition, SVD, eigendecomposition, or other non-GPU-friendly primitive is invoked, consistent with the design constraints stated at the start of Section 2.

The total number of matrix-matrix products across the online stage scales as O(T*d) for T iterations of degree-d polynomials (concretely, three products per degree-5 iteration under Horner's rule), consistent with the cost accounting in Section 2 following equation (4).

The precomputed coefficient tuples are consumed in schedule order, so that iteration t uses the coefficients derived for interval [l_t, u_t]. Reversing or shuffling the schedule must change the result.

The online stage runs in bfloat16: the input matrix is cast to bfloat16 before iterating and all intermediate iterates remain in bfloat16, consistent with Section 3.5's statement that the online stage can be performed in lower precision for greater speed on a GPU.

Implementation 1's transpose optimization is reproduced: if the input has more rows than columns the matrix is transposed before iterating (reducing the size of the Gram matrix X^T X and hence the FLOP count), and the output is transposed back before being returned.

When the requested number of steps exceeds the length of the stored coefficient list, the final coefficient tuple is repeated for the remaining steps, as Implementation 1 does via itertools.repeat. This is correct because the schedule has already converged to the fixed Newton-Schulz coefficients by that point.

The online routine accepts inputs with ndim >= 2 and applies the iteration over the trailing two dimensions, so that stacks of matrices can be processed together, as Implementation 1 does via the .mT transpose and dim=(-2, -1) norm.
The online routine is wrapped in torch.compile as in Implementation 1, so the polynomial iteration is fused into a compiled kernel.

The online routine exposes a signature taking a matrix and a step count and returning an approximation to polar(M) of the same shape, with no dependencies besides PyTorch, so that it is a drop-in replacement for existing matrix sign implementations such as Jordan's, You's, and Modula's, as claimed in Section 1.3 and Appendix A.
The recommended degree d = 5 is the default configuration for deep learning use, as recommended in Section 3.5.
The recommended iteration count T = 5 or T = 6 is the default configuration for deep learning use, as recommended in Section 3.5.

For a test matrix M, the output of the online stage after T iterations is verified to approximate polar(M) = U*V^T computed from a reference SVD, with spectral norm error consistent with the offline bound 1 - l_{T+1}.

The baseline matrix sign methods that Polar Express is compared against have been implemented: degree-5 Newton-Schulz, the degree-3 Newton-Schulz iteration of equation (2), Jordan et al. (2024b)'s heuristic quintic, and You's six-step method (Cesista et al., 2025). All are polynomial iterations using only matrix-matrix products, exposed through a common interface.

Degree-5 Newton-Schulz is implemented as a FIXED polynomial iteration applying p(x) = (15x - 10x^3 + 3x^5)/8 at every iteration, i.e. X_{t+1} = (15*X_t - 10*X_t*(X_t^T X_t) + 3*X_t*(X_t^T X_t)^2)/8, using only matrix-matrix products.
The classical degree-3 Newton-Schulz iteration of equation (2) is implemented: X_0 = M / ||M||_F and X_{t+1} = (3/2)X_t - (1/2)X_t X_t^T X_t.
Jordan et al. (2024b)'s method uses exactly the coefficients p(x) = 3.4445x - 4.7750x^3 + 2.0315x^5 as stated in Section 1.2.
Jordan's polynomial is applied unchanged at every iteration (a fixed-point iteration), not adapted per step.

You's method (Cesista et al., 2025) is implemented as a succession of six DIFFERENT degree-5 polynomial updates, each with its own coefficients found by heuristic search, applied in the prescribed order.

You's method is only defined for six iterations and the implementation does not extrapolate a seventh or later update from it, consistent with Section 1.2 and with Figure 3, where the You curve terminates at iteration 6.

All baseline methods and Polar Express share a single call signature (matrix in, approximate polar factor out) so that switching methods requires changing only one argument or function reference, both in the convergence experiments and inside the Muon optimizer.
All methods being compared start from the same normalized initial iterate derived from the same input matrix, so that per-iteration error comparisons are not confounded by different initializations.

Jordan's fixed polynomial is verified not to converge to polar(M): iterating it far beyond the number of steps used in training leaves a residual error that stops decreasing, consistent with Section 1.2's statement that it plateaus at an error of approximately 0.3.
Degree-5 Newton-Schulz is verified to converge to polar(M) when iterated sufficiently many times (unlike Jordan's and You's methods), consistent with Section 1.2.

The convergence experiments comparing Polar Express against Newton-Schulz, Jordan, and You have been reproduced: the main spectral norm comparison of Figure 3 on synthetic and GPT-2 gradient matrices, and the supplementary Frobenius/cosine (Figure 8) and truncated-spectrum (Figure 10) analyses of Appendix H.1.

The two families of test matrices used in Section 4.1 have been constructed: a synthetic matrix with logarithmically spaced singular values spanning six orders of magnitude, and real gradient matrices extracted from a randomly-initialized GPT-2 model on batches of language modeling data.
A synthetic test matrix is constructed whose singular values are evenly spaced on a logarithmic scale between 1e-6 and 1, so that sigma_max = 1 and sigma_min = 1e-6 as stated in the Figure 3 caption.
The singular vectors of the synthetic matrix are chosen randomly (a random orthonormal basis), so the matrix is a random matrix with a prescribed spectrum rather than a diagonal matrix.

The non-synthetic test matrix for the right panel of Figure 3 is the gradient of the mlp.c_proj weight matrix in the fourth transformer block of a randomly-initialized GPT-2 model, evaluated on a batch of language modeling data, as pinned by the Figure 3 caption and panel title.
The GPT-2 gradient experiment is repeated over 20 distinct batches of language modeling data so that a distribution over gradient matrices is obtained, as stated in the Figure 3 caption.
The GPT-2 model used to produce the test gradients is randomly initialized (not a pretrained checkpoint), as specified in the Figure 3 caption.

Three degree-5 Polar Express variants with different lower bound guesses are instantiated for Figure 3, spanning two orders of magnitude on either side of the true sigma_min = 1e-6 of the synthetic matrix: l = 1e-6 (exact), l = 1e-4 (two orders too large), and l = 1e-8 (two orders too small).
A Polar Express variant is built with l = 1e-6, which exactly matches sigma_min of the synthetic test matrix, by running the offline stage with that lower bound to obtain its own polynomial schedule.
A Polar Express variant is built with l = 1e-4, two orders of magnitude LARGER than the true sigma_min = 1e-6, with its own offline schedule.
A Polar Express variant is built with l = 1e-8, two orders of magnitude SMALLER than the true sigma_min = 1e-6, with its own offline schedule.
For the GPT-2 gradient convergence plots of Appendix H.1 (Figures 8 and 10), a Polar Express variant with the deployment default l = 1e-3 is used, matching the legends of those figures.

The error metrics used across the convergence experiments have been implemented: spectral norm error against an exact SVD-derived polar factor (Figure 3), and relative Frobenius error plus cosine similarity in the Frobenius inner product (Figure 8).

Convergence in Figure 3 is measured as the spectral norm error ||polar(M) - X_t||_2, where polar(M) = U*V^T is the exact polar factor obtained from a full SVD of the test matrix and X_t is the iterate after t polynomial applications.
A relative Frobenius norm error metric is implemented for Figure 8, measuring ||polar(M) - X_t||_F normalized by ||polar(M)||_F.
A cosine similarity metric is implemented for Figure 8 with respect to the Frobenius inner product <A, B> = Tr(A^T B), i.e. <A, B>_F / (||A||_F * ||B||_F), as defined in Appendix H.1.
The chosen error metric is recorded after every iteration for every method, producing per-iteration convergence traces rather than only a final error value.

Figure 3 has been reproduced: a two-panel comparison of degree-5 polynomial methods measured in spectral norm error versus iteration count, on the synthetic log-spaced matrix (left, out to 25 iterations, log y-axis) and on GPT-2 gradients (right, out to 10 iterations, linear y-axis with a shaded 90 percent interval over 20 batches).

The convergence comparison is executed for all six curves in the Figure 3 legend (Newton-Schulz d=5, Jordan, You, and Polar Express at l = 1e-8, 1e-6, 1e-4) on both test matrices, with error logged at every iteration.

The Muon optimizer of Section 1.1 has been implemented: a momentum buffer updated as M_t = beta*M_{t-1} + (1-beta)*G_t with M_0 = 0 and beta = 0.9, a weight update W_{t+1} = W_t - lambda*polar(M_t) that steps along the orthogonalized momentum, a pluggable polar factor routine, and the nano-gpt parameter assignment policy that routes excluded parameters to AdamW.

The spectrum-aware initialization scheme of Appendix I has been implemented and evaluated (Figure 17): for matrices with large spectral gaps, subspace iteration is used to bracket the leading singular values and a specially constructed cubic preprocesses the matrix so that the large outlying singular values are handled before the standard iteration begins.

Subspace iteration is implemented as described in footnote 10 of Appendix I: starting from a random Q_0 with orthonormal columns, repeatedly compute Q_{t+1}, R_{t+1} = qr(M^T M Q_t), then take the singular values of M Q_T as the estimates.
The subspace iteration estimates are used as LOWER bounds sigma_tilde_i <= sigma_i, justified in Appendix I by the Cauchy interlacing theorem.

Upper bounds on each leading singular value are computed from the Frobenius norm identity of equation (24): sigma_i <= sqrt(||M||_F^2 - sum_{j != i, j <= k} sigma_tilde_j^2), which also bounds the tail sigma_{k+1}, ..., sigma_n when i = k+1.

For the k = 1 case the preprocessing cubic p(x) = a*x + b*x^3 is constructed with the coefficients of equation (25), a = (z^2*(z + sqrt(1 - z^2)) - sqrt(1 - z^2)) / (z*sqrt(1 - z^2)*(2*z^2 - 1)) and b = (sqrt(1 - z^2) - z) / (z*sqrt(1 - z^2)*(2*z^2 - 1)), where z = sigma_tilde_1 and M is normalized so that ||M||_F = 1.
The constructed cubic is verified to satisfy the two interpolation conditions used to derive equation (25): p(sqrt(1 - z^2)) = 1 and p(z) = 1.
The scheme is applied only when the bracketing intervals do not overlap, i.e. when sqrt(1 - z^2) <= z, equivalently z >= 1/sqrt(2), as required in Appendix I.
The Figure 17 test matrix is a 32x32 synthetic matrix with power-law decaying spectrum sigma_j(M) = j^{-5}, so that it has a single large outlying singular value, as stated in the Figure 17 caption.

Because applying the initialization costs about as much as one degree-5 iteration, it is counted as an additional iteration when plotting convergence, as stated explicitly in Appendix I and in the Figure 17 caption, so the comparison is not artificially favorable.

Convergence is measured for four configurations on the power-law test matrix: Newton-Schulz and Polar Express, each with standard and with spectrum-aware initialization, with spectral error logged per iteration out to 25 iterations.
Figure 17 is plotted as spectral error versus iteration for the four configurations, with method distinguished by color and initializer distinguished by line style.
Figure 17 shows that spectrum-aware initialization significantly speeds convergence for BOTH Newton-Schulz and Polar Express on the power-law test matrix, as stated in Appendix I.

The fast polynomial iteration for rectangular matrices of Appendix J has been reproduced: Algorithm 3 and its numerical stabilizations, the GPU runtime benchmark of Figure 18, and the application to Muon by splitting attention weight matrices per head described in Appendix J.1.

Algorithm 3 of Appendix J has been implemented: for a tall matrix, the entire T-iteration polynomial composition is computed using only two rectangular matrix multiplications by propagating a small square factor Q_t instead of the full iterate.
The Gram matrix Y = X^T X is formed once before the loop at a cost of m*n^2, as in Algorithm 3.
The propagated factor is initialized as Q_0 = I of size n x n, as in Algorithm 3.
At each iteration the small matrix is updated as R_t = Q_{t-1}^T Y Q_{t-1} at a cost of 2*n^3, as in Algorithm 3.

At each iteration the propagated factor is updated as Q_t = Q_{t-1} * h_t(R_t), where h_t is the degree-q polynomial satisfying p_t(x) = x*h_t(x^2), evaluated by Horner's rule at a cost of deg(h_t)*n^3, as in Algorithm 3.
The result is returned as X * Q_T, the second and final rectangular multiplication, at a cost of m*n^2, as in Algorithm 3.

The inner loop contains no rectangular matrix multiplications; only the pre-loop Gram matrix and the post-loop product involve the large dimension m, which is the entire point of the algorithm as stated in Appendix J.

The implementation is verified to reproduce the baseline result, i.e. X*Q_T equals (p_T o ... o p_1)(X) to numerical tolerance, following the induction of equations (26) and (27) that R_t = r_t(X) and Q_t = q_t(X).
The algorithm is applied only to inputs with m > 1.5*n, as required by the input condition of Algorithm 3.

The choice between Algorithm 3 and the baseline is made at runtime by the cost criterion of Appendix J: Algorithm 3 is cheaper when the aspect ratio satisfies alpha > 1.5*T/(T-1), derived from the total cost ((d+3)/2 * T + 2*alpha) * n^3.

The restarting strategy of Appendix J is implemented: Algorithm 3 is applied over blocks of three iterations at a time (X_0 -> X_3 -> X_6 -> ...) rather than for all T iterations at once, because Q_T becomes ill-conditioned for large T when X has very small singular values.

On the first application of Algorithm 3 the Gram matrix is regularized as Y = X^T X + 1e-3 * I to prevent round-off from introducing spurious negative eigenvalues that would cause divergence; subsequent restarts use Y = X^T X unmodified, as specified in Appendix J.
When the ridge regularization is applied the input is correspondingly normalized by ||X||_F + 1e-3 rather than by ||X||_F, as stated in Appendix J.

The reproduction reflects Appendix J's argument that adding 1e-3 * I to the Gram matrix slightly increases each singular value but does NOT change the polar factor of X, so the algorithm still converges to the correct answer despite differing in the early iterations.

The observation of footnote 11 is verified or documented: Q_T tends to Y^{-1/2}, so the Polar Express polynomials also yield a method for computing the inverse square root of a positive semidefinite matrix.
